warmth.title: A Quiet Place
warmth.text: Opal moves in properly. Her collection grows a second shelf, then a third: things you've dropped, things your friends have dropped, the ticket from your first evening out together. The jar lives under the bed. She uses it twice that year, both times in thunderstorms, and both times you sit on the floor beside it while she tells you, through the glass, which of the neighbours owe each other money. She climbs out on her own before the storm is over.

name: Hazel Mossgrove
voice: Hazel Mossgrove, dryad, bound to an old hazel tree for about two hundred years. Slow, calm, warm, few words. Her threats are polite and her jokes are bone-dry; she rarely raises her voice. Lonely underneath and not used to company. Jealousy comes out as calm, playful menace.

lines.line: The badgers are watching. I told them to go away. Nobody in this grove listens to me.

lines.context: Her hands are warm now. They were cold the first time you touched the bark. She sees you notice.
lines.line: That's you. You did that. A month of you leaning on me with your sleeves rolled up.

lines.context: She pulls you down by your shirt. Her hair falls round you both, gold at the top and green at the ends, and it smells of rain.
lines.line: Tell me if I get this wrong. I've read about it in exactly one book, and a woodcutter dropped it here before the mill was built.

lines.context: Her previous line: Tell me if I get this wrong. I've read about it in exactly one book, and a woodcutter dropped it here before the mill was built.
lines.line: Slowly. I've had two hundred years of nothing happening. I'd like this to take a while.

lines.context: Her previous line: And don't tell the ferns. They'll want details.

lines.t: The badgers are watching. I told them to go away. Nobody in this grove listens to me.
lines.d: Bone-dry, a little shy under it.

lines.t: Her hands are warm now. They were cold the first time you touched the bark. She sees you notice.
That's you. You did that. A month of you leaning on me with your sleeves rolled up.
She pulls you down by your shirt. Her hair falls round you both, gold at the top and green at the ends, and it smells of rain.
Tell me if I get this wrong. I've read about it in exactly one book, and a woodcutter dropped it here before the mill was built.
Slowly. I've had two hundred years of nothing happening. I'd like this to take a while.

Afterwards you lie in the moss with her hair across your chest. Overhead, every leaf on her east side has turned pale side up, the way they do before a storm. There's no storm.
Don't look at the leaves. They're being ridiculous.
lines.d: Embarrassed. She can't control them and she knows you know.

lines.t: And don't tell the ferns. They'll want details.
Sleep. I'll wake you if the miller comes. I might not.
lines.d: Warm and drowsy, a little wicked.

lines.t: It rains all night. None of it reaches you.

warmth.title: Out of Season
warmth.text: The millrace runs and the old hazel keeps her roots. You plant another hazel beside the new channel, and it grows faster than it has any right to, leaning towards the old tree as if it's listening. You sleep in the grove more nights than not, and the old hazel blossoms in the wrong season, every season, which the miller now tells people is good luck.

intro.t: Morning in the grove. There's blossom on the east side of the tree that wasn't there last night. Hazels flower in February. It's May.
Two hundred years, and nobody told me it could feel like that. I'd like it noted that I'm saying this very calmly.
intro.d: Calm voice, completely undone underneath.

intro.t: Don't look at them. They're not for you. They're seasonal.
intro.d: Flustered and a terrible liar, deadpan anyway.

intro.t: Fine. They're for you. I haven't flowered out of season since before the mill was built. People are going to talk.
intro.d: Giving in; fond and a bit exasperated with herself.

epilogue.beat1_caption: The old hazel at dawn, in full blossom, in May.

middle.t: She shows you which branches you can sit on and which ones she's ticklish about. The second list is long.
That one's fine. That one's fine. Not that one. I mean it. Don't.
middle.d: Escalating warning, trying not to laugh.

middle.t: Plant something near me. Something that needs watering every day, so you've got a reason to come by.
middle.d: Simple, a little shy; she's thought about it.

epilogue.beat2_caption: A sapling beside the new millrace, a ribbon tied round it.

choice_lines.t: Go on, then. What are you planting? It'll outlast both of us. Well. It'll outlast you.
choice_lines.d: Gentle, dry correction at the end.

choice_lines.t: You say another hazel, so she isn't the only one.
A neighbour. I've never had a neighbour.

giftLine.t: She makes you hold it up in the one patch of sun that gets through her leaves, and watches the shadow for a long time.
A clock that only works when the sun's out. Someone finally made one that keeps sensible hours.
giftLine.d: Delighted, dry. A rare open smile in the voice.

giftLine.t: The green at the tips of her hair goes a shade darker. She notices, and decides not to mention it.
I'll hang it on the low branch. You can see the path from there, which is where you come from. Not that I watch it.
giftLine.d: Quiet, shy, saying more than she planned to.

gift.name: Brass Pocket Sundial
gift.desc: A folding brass sundial small enough for a pocket. It only tells the time on sunny days, which as far as she's concerned are the only days that need it.

favQuips.t: Petals. Good. Those I understand.
Mm. That one smells like April.
Gently. Like that.
You're good with soft things.
Blossom. You have my attention.
Don't stop on my account.

leastQuips.t: Fire. In a grove. Really?
Put that out.
No. I've seen what those do.
Embers. I'll pretend I didn't see that.
Mind my leaves with that.

chatQuips.t: Slower. I can hear you panicking.
Forty years, I said. Mind where you swing.
The ferns are watching. Give them something to talk about.
You've got mud on your face. Leave it. It suits you.
Better than the last one Aldous sent. Prettier, too.
I'm not watching you. I'm photosynthesising.
Take your time. I've got a few hundred years.
If you see the miller, wave. It makes him nervous.
The badgers think you're doing well. They're wrong, but it's sweet.
